from math import comb
n=2; threshold=0.75
W=[(0,0),(1,1)]
outputs=list(product((0,1), repeat=n))
hits=sum(max(sum(a==b for a,b in zip(x,w))/n for w in W)>=threshold for x in outputs)

# Construct the primitive binary BCH code of length 63 and designed distance 21.
# GF(64) uses primitive polynomial x"'^6 + x + 1.
def mul(a,b):
 out=0
 while b:
  if b&1: out''^=a
  b>>=1
  a<<=1
  if a&64: a''^=0x43
 return out
alpha=[1]
for i in range(1,63): alpha.append(mul(alpha[-1],2))
assert len(set(alpha))==63 and mul(alpha[-1],2)==1
roots=set()
for i in range(1,21):
 j=i
 while j not in roots:
  roots.add(j);j=(2*j)%63
p=[1]
for r in sorted(roots):
 q=[0]*(len(p)+1)
 for i,c in enumerate(p):
  q[i]''^=mul(c,alpha[r]);q[i+1]''^=c
 p=q
assert all(c in (0,1) for c in p)
g=sum(c<<i for i,c in enumerate(p))
k=63-(len(p)-1)
# Enumerate all nonzero codewords using Gray-code transitions.
code=0;prev=0;minimum=64
for i in range(1,1<<k):
 gray=i''^(i>>1)
 changed=gray''^prev
 code''^=g<<(changed.bit_length()-1)
 weight=code.bit_count()
 extended_weight=weight+(weight&1)
 minimum=min(minimum,extended_weight)
 prev=gray
print({'"'length_with_parity':64,'dimension':k,'codewords':1<<k,'minimum_distance_verified':minimum,'maximum_pairwise_bit_agreement':(64-minimum)/64})
PY"

from itertools import product
W=((0,0),(1,1)); beta=0.7; threshold=0.6
TDR=TAR=0
for y in product((0,1),repeat=2):
 p=1
 for bit in y:p*=beta if bit==0 else 1-beta
 score=[sum(a==b for a,b in zip(y,w))/2 for w in W]
 if max(score)>=threshold:
  TDR+=p
  if score[0]>score[1]:TAR+=p
print({'detection_implies_attribution_counterexample':{'n':2,'s':2,'beta':beta,'tau':threshold,'max_agreement_between_watermarks':0,'TDR':TDR,'TAR':TAR}})

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: attributing generated content to registered users beyond merely detecting a service’s watermark. The proposed registration, embedding, and attribution pipeline is clearly explained.

The image experiments cover three generators, 100,000 users by default, and a scaling experiment with one million users. Clean-image results are strong, and reporting worst-user performance, post-processing results, and initialization ablations is useful.

The Hamming-distance formulation provides an understandable connection between watermark separation and attribution. The paper also explicitly acknowledges that its robustness depends on the underlying watermarking method, including failure under white-box attacks.
weaknesses: Novelty and baselines are insufficiently established relative to classical digital fingerprinting and error-correcting codes. A-BSTA mainly truncates an existing search algorithm and changes its initialization, without an approximation guarantee. A particularly relevant missing baseline is an extended binary BCH [64,18,22] code: it supplies 262,144 distinct watermarks with maximum pairwise agreement at most 0.65625, better than A-BSTA’s reported 0.734 on the paper’s geometric objective. Evaluating such constructions is essential to establish the proposed algorithm’s value.

The false-detection guarantee has a substantive independence problem. Appendix D factors probabilities of comparisons that share the same decoded watermark; this is unjustified for a fixed selected database. For example, with watermarks {00,11}, independent uniform decoded bits, and threshold 0.75, the actual FDR is 0.5, whereas Equation 11 gives 0.4375. Independently sampling a random codebook requires distinguishing an average-over-codebooks guarantee from a guarantee for the deployed database. Moreover, Section 6.6 applies Theorem 3 to A-BSTA watermarks, although their selection is explicitly dependent.

The claim in Section 5.5 that detection implies attribution does not follow from approximately matching lower bounds on TDR and TAR. A decoded watermark can fall near another user’s watermark and therefore be detected but incorrectly attributed, even when the stated separation condition holds. An explicit bound on misattribution probability is needed.

The theoretical connection to actual neural watermarking remains weak. Definitions 3–4 require independent decoded bits, with identical correctness probabilities for watermarked content. These assumptions are not empirically validated, especially after post-processing. Estimating average bit accuracy on the same test images and observing agreement of aggregate rates does not validate the binomial model or its tail guarantees. The description of estimating gamma also does not establish the per-position bias bound required by Definition 4.

The false-positive evaluation is inadequate for the proposed forensic application. Only 1,000 unwatermarked images are tested; even zero false detections would give a one-sided 95% upper confidence limit of approximately 0.003. Thus, the reported near-zero empirical FDR does not establish sufficiently rare false accusations at deployment scale. Independent calibration, larger negative sets, and uncertainty estimates are needed.

Robustness and fidelity evidence are incomplete. Common transformations largely match those used during training, and the adversarial evaluation uses only WEvade-B-Q. This does not establish broader black-box robustness or resistance to attribution-specific attacks such as collusion and framing. Images are restricted to 128×128, and reported SSIM measures post-processing damage rather than the original-to-watermarked distortion, leaving the quality cost of robust embedding unclear.

The text experiment uses Wikipedia test segments rather than actual language-model outputs. It also increases the watermark loss weight substantially without evaluating fluency or semantic preservation. Testing a length-constrained paraphraser after training against paraphrasing supports a limited text-watermarking demonstration, but not the broader claim of reliable attribution of AI-generated text.
